name: Domaine Gourt de Mautens (Jérôme Bressy) Vaucluse Rouge 2015
text:
## Domaine Gourt de Mautens (Jérôme Bressy) Vaucluse Rouge 2015

**The story.** The estate sits in [Rasteau](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Rasteau,+Vaucluse,+France&t=k), in the southern Rhône. Jérôme Bressy founded it in 1996, at 23, making his first vintage in a converted hangar on his parents' farm. His family had long sold grapes to the local cooperative. In 1989 his father Yves converted the vineyards to organic farming. Jérôme completed biodynamic certification in 2008.

The label says Vaucluse, not Rasteau, for a reason. In 2010, Rasteau became its own appellation with tighter rules on grape varieties. Bressy refused to change his blend and left, labelling the wines IGP Vaucluse. The broader département is at [Vaucluse](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Vaucluse,+Provence,+France&t=k).

**The blend.** The 2015 is about 50% Grenache, with Mourvèdre, Carignan, Counoise, Vaccarèse, Cinsault, Syrah and Terret Noir. Jancis Robinson notes vines of 50 to 100 years and a 2015 yield of about 12 hl/ha.

**What the critics say for 2015.**
- **Jeb Dunnuck:** 97 points (October 2017). He compared it to the Chambolle-Musigny of the Rhône, meaning pure and elegant rather than heavy.
- **Decanter:** Matt Walls also gave 97 points. He described a lively, expressive wine with firm tannins and a grippy finish. He said it carries its alcohol without tasting unbalanced.
- **Jancis Robinson:** 16.5/20 (September 2019). That is a more reserved score. She found it big, rich and sweet, with fairly dry tannins, and said it needs food.
- **CellarTracker:** 93.6 average across 56 reviews on the page I found. Your list says 93.35, so the figure may have moved. Individual notes vary, from Eric Guido's 97 in 2018 to two 90s in 2020 and 2021. Those two notes cite ripe sweetness, alcohol and firm tannin.

**Practical note.** Critics disagree on timing. Dunnuck expects maturity between 2017 and 2030. Robinson felt it was drinkable in 2019, and the producer says wines like this can be cellared for about 20 years. One CellarTracker taster in 2021 found the tannins still aggressive and wanted a long decant. I'd decant for one to two hours and drink it with food. Lamb, venison or a hard cheese would suit it. A CellarTracker page lists lamb, venison and hard cheese among its pairings.

**An aside on the name and soils.** "Gourt" means a place where water flows, and "Mautens" means storm or bad weather. The water runs in storms, so roots reach moisture even in dry years. Dunnuck notes the fruit comes from clay and limestone soils around Rasteau.

**From the history books**
- 1989: Yves Bressy converts the family vines to organic farming.
- 1996: Jérôme Bressy makes the first Gourt de Mautens vintage. [Rasteau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:Search?search=Rasteau+AOC&go=Go)
- 2010: Rasteau is promoted to its own appellation, and Bressy leaves it. [Appellation d'origine contrôlée](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:Search?search=Appellation+d%27origine+contr%C3%B4l%C3%A9e&go=Go)
